title: Zen and Creativity Class 1
speaker: Shuko Edie Norton
summary: Shuko Edie Norton opens a class called Zen and Creativity by explaining that zazen mind can shape how people make things, with attention on the process and not the product. Shuko describes plein air watercolor and poetry as practice, then guides a visualization and has everyone shape clay inside a bag without looking. Participants share the scenes they modeled: a hayloft ladder at Uncle Frank's farm, turtles in a rainy park beside the Yangtze, a motorcycle ride through the Tucson desert, humpback whales bubble net fishing. The second half turns to therapeutic touch, where partners feel the energy between their hands, then work with an intention the receiver names, and the class ends with plans to meet at Shuko's house on the 12th and bring photographs.

sentences.text: Welcome to this class on Zen perception.
Let's say our names first of all.
Tim will be here at our next meeting, and also Nancy, who had work today, so she's going to do a makeup on Monday.
This is a class in which we're going to explore how our zazen mind helps us express ourselves creatively.
We'll use various media: clay today, words, pastels, crayons, song, movement, lots of different ways.
The goal of this class is not the product.
Our focus is not on what we create or produce but on the process of creating: how we approach and work with the media, and what we experience as we make something.
Now, I'm aware that some people might feel nervous about doing art if they believe they have no artistic skills or previous experience.
And it's true that there is a little risk in trying to express ourselves in a group without really knowing ahead of time what's going to happen.
But what I hope we can do is support each other in taking these little risks, just as we support each other in zazen.
Taking a risk is a natural part of creative expression.
In creating something, a picture or a dance, we don't know ahead of time how exactly it's going to come out.
And we tap into deeper resources of our minds and bodies, I feel, than just our ordinary thinking mind.
We tap into our unconscious awareness, the part of us to which zazen mind has access.
The idea of this class comes from my observation, over many years, of how the focus and spaciousness of zazen mind has helped me with my own creative expression in painting.

I noticed that in preparation for [unclear: "writing"] a painting, for instance, if I settle myself down into zazen, present and grounded, I can observe my subject much more clearly and come closer to expressing what it is I intended.
For instance, I love to do plein air watercolor.

Arranging to do it is something of a challenge, because I'm usually busy with other things, and then sometimes it shouldn't be too cold, it shouldn't be raining of course, and it can't be too windy because the watercolor dries too quickly.
So the number of days that I can go outside and paint are few and far between.

I have found also that if I go out on a day when I'm going someplace else afterwards or coming back from someplace, and I'm rushed and I'm thinking about that goal, I can't settle down into the zazen mind that I really need to see clearly.
So often in those circumstances I find that my experience is unsatisfying.
I've discovered how much more deeply I experience the scenes that I visit by drawing or painting them.
Then when I'm home, even though, all things considered, they're not all good paintings, they remind me of how deeply I experience those places, so I've enjoyed that a lot.
It is true for poetry writing.
I do best when I take the time needed really to allow my attention to dwell on and play with the subject, whatever subject it is that I'm wanting to write about.
The spaciousness of awareness that zazen permits is really necessary.
Creativity can be defined as bringing into existence something for the first time, making something new and unique.
I always find that it's the uniqueness of a work of art that [unclear: "so I always wonder"] how did that person ever think of doing that?
It's really new to me.
So none of us may be artists officially. [unclear: "I've just taken and so"] the expression of our creativity is art.
Certainly it is a creative.

I subtitled this course because of the obvious reference to the Heart Sutra, but also because I have found my experiences in expressing myself creatively are ones in which I actually feel little or no separation between the scene, the image in my mind, my paintings and poems.
Good, not all that much.
Some are okay, but in some way when I do it in this manner, they're really satisfying to me.
I can see, "Oh, I like that little part very much."
I really got the process, and I really do, in any form of creativity.
I'm not so interested in experiencing.
So I'm hoping that you all will observe and reflect on what you're doing as you're doing it, and that you will have this sensation of no separation from what you're creating.
So in this class today, I want you to think about these things.
Use your experience in zazen to settle and focus your mind.
Extend bodhisattva mind to yourself and others as we work together.
Forget about perfection.
Believe that you will learn from whatever the outcome is, and breathe through the process.
Today we're going to start with the sense of touch.
The first thing we're going to do is work with clay, and the second thing we'll do is work with hands on, explore what our sense of touch is, both with clay.
To set up for this experience we're going to do a guided meditation first.
So I want you to get in a comfortable position that you can stay in for this time, and close your eyes.
A scene that you will explore, and from which you will think of some object that you want to make with clay.
So I want you to visualize a place, a scene in which you have felt very alive, or some other that to your mind.
First of all, what do you see in the scene?
Own or with other people or animals, bees or plants, or in this scene, shapes, or any sounds?
If so, smell anything, any sensation on yourself.
What are you doing in the scene?
This scene for a person or being that you might want to use to represent to yourself the scene.

So the idea here is to, and you actually have to work with it a little bit, once you feel like it's possible to work with it, bag and work without looking at it to make something that represents the scene.
So don't get into a shape yet before you shape it.
Okay?
We're going to try and just focus on actually shapes coming out here.
Looking at it, can we put our hands in there?
Yeah, that's what you're supposed to do.
Put your hands in the bag.
You're doing something and you go, "Well, I'm not that interested."
What was it like, and briefly explain what kind of scene it was that you were in?
Sure.
I remember when we went to the Old Grove, and afterwards we were standing there, or maybe when we were, was that Leah?
Yeah, she was dancing in the water pool.
That's great.
How did it feel to you, making it without seeing it?
It was hard.
I mean, it was hard.
I could feel myself wanting it.
The scene was when I was a child and we used to go to my Uncle Frank's farm.
There was this place, and we would play in the hayloft.
We would be way high up, it seemed, way high up off the ground floor.
And there would be this ladder that we would go up and down.
It would be really scary, and we'd have each other around to go up and down the ladder.
An amazing ladder.
It was amazing to work with you in this way.
It was actually very good, I felt.
And so I didn't feel plugged into the results of the product at all.
I just got into the process.
So I enjoy it, really enjoy it.
Two summers ago I backpacked through China and Laos for a great Buddhist historical places.
This was in Lishan, which is known for the largest Buddha in the world.
And they have a park there next to the Buddha that was not really known very well in the tourist scene.
So I got to go to this park, and in it there was a section on a hill, and below it was, I think it was the Yangtze River, which is a huge river, which makes this rumbling noise all the time.
It was a section that was almost like mosaic tiles, and then a bamboo forest that came up above, and seating where a sage would go and write a long time ago.
I don't remember his name, but there was a pond running through and a bridge, and in the pond were turtles.
It was one of the most serene places I've ever been.
I was the only one there, and it was quiet and it was raining.
And so the turtles were in the water, looking up.
Yeah, playing with the clay was great.
I could tell when I was trying to shape, especially the shell, it's more like a funny pancake maybe, but it's fun to rely on touch because you're never really sure what it's going to look like.
You can get the general shape, but yeah, it turned out alright.
Several things.
First of all, the process, I guess.
I really appreciate it, because any tendencies toward my usual obsessive-compulsive way of doing things are minimized, luckily, by this nice little barrier here.
So that was good, and it's actually keeping in mind what I was trying to create.
So that was good.
So, this is supposed to be a scene up by, I believe the place, it's up Mount Baker's.
And so we have Shuksan in the back here.
Any number of these depressions that either have snow or water in them at the right time.
We have the trail coming up and out.
We have the valley over here.
I did the whole scene.
It all just goes down that way.
It's all bent down and so on and so on.
But what it is is, we've had family and friends up there a number of times, and down this side to get some huckleberries, and valleys here.
Just was, in order to do it, take the shape of my hand.
You know what I mean?
There's only so much you can do that isn't affected by whatever our physicality is.
Everybody's artwork is different, any medium.
When I was 18, I had the privilege of hiking with a friend who was hiking from Mexico to Canada on the Continental Divide.
I joined up with her for a month, in Northern Colorado.
And we hiked into Wyoming, and we hiked into the Great Basin.
Then we hiked out of the Great Basin into the Wind River Mountain Range.
I hiked through the Wind Rivers with her and got off the trail because I needed to go to college.
On that trip, when we were in the Great Basin, it was just phenomenal.
There were so many colors of just greens and browns.
And not really greens.
Let's say browns, and different colors of browns.
But anyway, a few little greens.
But when we were hiking in the Great Basin, we had gotten almost all the way through it, and we came to this place where there were these twin buttes.

I climbed up on top of the butte, and I remember looking back the way we had come and then looking to the Wind Rivers, and these are the Wind Rivers here, and across the foothills that we were going to go through to get to the winds.
And I just remember being overcome by a sense of connection to everything.
I literally just dropped to my knees.
That was one of the most powerful experiences I've had, in just that sense that I was part of everything, and in awe of where I had come from and where we were going.
And I have never experienced that again.
Except now.

You know, it was really interesting, because I would go from being in my mind with the scene I was trying to create to being with the clay.
Either I was in my mind or I was with the clay.
But it was just fascinating to move back and forth between being with the clay and being in my mind with this image.
I can't lift it up.
Actually, happy accident.
I think the bag is part of the scene.
During the whole visualization, the real element that I was remembering was the atmosphere in the air.
It's hard to do in clay.
Exactly, exactly, right.
And also I was being a little non-specific during the visualization about various times.
But then I did focus on this one time.
They were all similar times.
It's all about when I used to live in Tucson and how the air would be during the sunset a lot of times in the desert, and just what life was like there at that period of time.
But I did focus on this one memory of taking a motorcycle trip with a girlfriend.
And so this is us on the motorcycle going through the desert with the mountains in the background.
And then this is all just how the air felt.

With the plastic bag.

Soft and silky.

That's great.
Any reflections on doing the process?
Oh, doing the process was really interesting.
Yeah, the first thing I did was just establish the earth.
So there's this sense of just, because what I was trying to do was build it all up from some lower level.
I really enjoyed not being able to, and not even trying to, use my eyes, and just being able to feel.
Mine, I was visualizing a time a few years ago when I was on a trip on the Inside Passage in a smallish boat, a 54-foot boat.
We came upon several pods of humpback whales that were bubble net fishing.
It was so thrilling to see them go up and so forth.
So this is my whale, several times amidst several pods.
It was really so precious to share our lives with such huge lives.
It was brilliant.
And working with the clay, what I noticed in myself, and also in all of you because I was looking out at all of you, is we were all visualizing really hard.
I think that's part of how we get no separation from the thing that we're making: we're really thinking hard about it.
We're trying to see it.
And you can have that experience best when you're really not using your eyes.
You're really one with it.
This clay dries hard and you can keep this.

You can do that.

I have plenty.

**Shuko Edie Norton:** So this next exercise isn't creative art, although it requires some creativity and maybe some art to it.
Therapeutic touch is an energy work type of massage therapy in a way.
Except for the most part you don't touch the person.
You feel the energy, and the idea of it is to move static energy or painful energy away from the body or down the body and out of the body and so forth.
So it's a very sensitive thing that you have to feel in your hands.
I'm just going to talk you through the initial touch of a person, and I'll tell you how we're going to do that.
But before we start I want you to experience the energy in your own hands.
So I want you to put your hands up in front of you about this far apart and focus on what you might feel.
Gradually move your hands closer together and see if you feel something in front of each other, and notice if and when you stop feeling it, and see if your sensation stops.
What did you discover in that?
What did you feel?
**Participant:** Like it was just concentration, more pulling away, I think, than moving towards.
When you try to bring your hand through water, that feeling of resistance and then also the pressure following you.
And so that's kind of what [unclear: "Enchigo and"] worked.
That sensation of pull to gauge where it stopped.
**Shuko Edie Norton:** That's a really good description of it.
I wouldn't have known how to describe it exactly the same way, but there was a sense of, yeah, this pressure, but at some point here it almost was sucking in.
It was much... and that's not the right word for it.
It was more like the sensation you would have as you were doing this under water.
It had a lot to do with the direction of the motion.
The quality of the sensation changed.
**Participant:** Like here it felt like there was a pulling and then pulling away.
For me it was like waves.
It was interesting because it was kind of like a pressure, so it was kind of pushing, but for the most part the waves just felt like they were like this.
And then when I moved to get it, it felt like they were like this.
So it was almost like containing energy.
I was just in my head using the word magnetism.
There's a magnetism there, kind of drawing in as you go out.
I get more of a feeling of solidity as I was moving in on it.
And of course warmth.
The heat increases as you go closer.
Then there was a point where there was a stopping point where it didn't want to go any further in or any further out.
Then it was almost like a natural movement on its own without my moving it.
Maybe that's the wave thing you're talking about.
I don't know.
It's hard to know.
**Shuko Edie Norton:** Other people explain it.
**Participant:** Can I add one comment?
That was really interesting.
I didn't exactly feel a wave thing myself, but what you were talking about reminded me of my high school physics class.
It's really interesting because my kid is in physics now and I went to the parent-teacher night and I mentioned this thing, and it was like some archaic thing.
I said, do you guys have wave tanks?
And he goes, "I got one up on the shelf."
We used to each have one in physics.
Now they do it on computers.
But I really think it's because the wave tank was a much more tactile, visual wave.

What it was was about an inch of water in a glass-bottomed tray that was on a stand that stood about this high off the table, and there was a white piece of paper and a light that shone down, and then there was a bar in the water with a little electric motor that would make the bar do this, and you could change the speed of it.

And that would make rolling sets of waves go across the tank, and when the waves hit the other side they would reflect back, and when they reflected back and hit the other waves it would create a standing static pattern of waves.

The light shining through where the waves were curved like this would be lenses, either focusing, so that on the paper you would see these bars of light and bars of shadow that were a certain distance apart that you could just measure.
Then if you increased it they got closer together, and decreased it they got the waves farther apart.
You were looking at physics, you were looking at pure energies and waves, and sort of showing how the distance created larger or closer together sets of wave patterns.
When you were describing that I just totally reflected on that.
**Shuko Edie Norton:** These energies that we're feeling here are of course all around us and in our bodies and so forth.
So in this energy work, in therapeutic touch, what the therapist is trying to do is feel, without touching the body, where in the body that energy is starting.
So you might come to somebody and you can feel it out here, so you wouldn't go any further in than that.
Or you might feel nothing there, a kind of emptiness, and so it needs some energy moved into it and so forth.
So it's using what our natural energy fields are, and they're different for different people in different circumstances and conditions and so forth.
So what I want to experiment with today is, for each in a partner, to first of all decide who's going to be the actor and who's going to be the receiver, and I think we'll have time to switch places.
Then talk to the receiver: what do you want to happen?
What intention do you have?
Do you want to feel peaceful, energized?
Do you want loss of pain if you're hurt some place?
What would be your intention for doing this?
The person thinks of that and says, this is my intention.
And so then the two of you have that intention, and particularly the person who's the giver, the actor, has that intention during the whole exercise to allow that to happen.
The person would lie down face up and would say, this is where I feel.
Mostly you would use just one hand, but you can use two if there's enough space in the person.
So as you first start, just the energy if you want to.
That takes some practice in doing and so forth, but it's okay to start with just a very gentle placing of the hand on the person and then thinking about hold, and just breathe into it.
Also, any sensation, you're just going to try to experience it.
And the person who's receiving, just notice any feelings that you have in that place where you're being touched or any place on your body.
So the actor focuses on the intention and what you receive, or just focuses on what they experience.
And this is again using our touch, not artistically exactly, except it's kind of an art to it, as you can imagine.
Just to become sensitive to that for a little bit.
So choose up partners, and I know not everybody knows everybody, but...
At one point you said that because of the energy you wouldn't necessarily click, but then you're saying...
We'll just start with touching, although you can play a little bit with the sensation of gently, but at the same time focus on whatever intention the person has.

Have that as the intention?
To have the energy flow?
Can that be the intention?
Can you say something more about intention?
**Shuko Edie Norton:** What the person would like to get out of it.
Moving... maybe you could say, rather than "move energy," "I want to feel energetic."
So you wouldn't have to move.
It might be easy to do.
**Participant:** Who figures out the place?
**Shuko Edie Norton:** The receiver.
This is where I feel.
Face up.
It's more vulnerable, I realize, but I think you'll receive it more.
So do...
**Participant:** I love when it starts not touching, and then I might move it back to support your neck.
Energetic, like it was a different feeling.
This is...

I felt mostly just like transfer of heat, and then that kind of like magnetic resistance, where we focusing mostly on using myself as a conductor, like transferring the energy out here through me to maybe open up blockages that create tension or whatever.
Like a lot of headaches, just like blood cells or whatever, like enlarge, like hitting the sides of my head and stuff, creating that tension.
I was just trying to focus on that, and then supporting your neck.

Like there's a stranger touching my head.

You know, it's not a big issue for me on that kind of level.
But it's more like just on the level of coming to terms with finding a layer where, oh, I'm being resistant.
Being aware of it, because the process makes you aware of it.
The process brings it out, you see that resistance.

I let go of a layer of resistance there, and that happened two or four times during the process, where I would realize that there was a little layer of resistance in the general acceptance that was going on, and I'd have to sort of consciously resist before accepting.
I could feel some of that too, because our bodies carry so much of that, like actually physically.
And so I felt you relax a few times.
Yeah, it's amazing how much, like, we don't even realize.
We think we're relaxed and then there's even more.
Yeah, the exchange seems to be the chest.
My joints get a lot of tension, physical, and so my knees have taken a lot of stress.
To relax my knees, if that's possible, and just kind of be aware of any pain that's there, so that I can...
Yeah, actually that's just... it just being aware of that.
**Shuko Edie Norton:** This general area you probably should do just on one, because it will be too much input for two.
Both of them will benefit even though you're touching only one.
So you might figure out which one you'd like.

I think actually what I felt the strongest was this sense, this kind of sense of relief that I didn't have to do this all by myself, that I wasn't doing it all for long.
Yeah, that we were working together and have felt some energy.
Yeah, yeah.
And in giving I felt some of what people talked about, energy-wise, waves of energy.
It was easier to feel doing that, then the energy seemed to be transmitting.
So after a while he mentioned that it was kind of... he felt it kind of moving out.

So then a little bit of, like, my nerves kind of felt... there's lots I could go on about, but I think the one thing when I was... need to move my other hand into another place, both terminals set, and decided against it just because of the pain she had.
I was supposed to be shifted from where my hand was to the other side.
And why?
Yeah, turns out that that's what was going on.
What was interesting is that I had a cramp put on Thursday on this side, and what ended up happening is it shifted.
So I had some pain and it shifted, but it was more shifted to pressure.
It was interesting because it literally shifted across my jaw, and that was fascinating.
The thing that I was noticing with Jeff, when I had my hand there, was I could feel my energy kind of flowing through him.
And then I of course was thinking about, as a psychologist, how I work with energy, but it's working with energy in kind of a verbal way, and how I can feel energy.
I can feel both my energy and the energy of the people I'm working with.
I have a sense of the energy, and how different it is to be laying on hands.
It's a different experience of the energy, and actually it was a little... to me it was easier to work with the energy of laying on hands.
It was just, for lack of a better word, more tactile.

But I could... it was just maybe because it's being contained with physicality, whereas in therapy it's just kind of an end... you know what I'm saying? [unclear: "I'm going to start laying on hands I don't joke just because I get fired"] at some level.
It was a substantially similar process.
Receiving was me discovering different layers of resistance, to notice them, and resistance to what was happening.
But then in the midst of my general receptiveness I would find these layers where there was a part of me that was reserving judgment.
And then in giving, I felt that I didn't want to try and manipulate what was going on or have some intention about manipulating what was going on.
I wanted to try and hold an acceptance of the situation.
I was finding it...
I moved my hand around as a way to sort of feel what the boundaries of the situation were, and sort of feel it more, not to change it but just to feel it.

It was more because I was just feeling like, I just want to accept what this is.
**Shuko Edie Norton:** Okay.
